title: Why a Code Matters
bigQuestion: What changes when a fighting practice gets a written rulebook?

story.title: A Page Says Begin
story.kicker: Two players in white and blue jackets wait for one word from the referee.
paragraphs: A big hall hums with voices. Square mats cover the floor. At the edge of one mat stand two judo players. One wears a white jacket. The other wears a blue one.

Each player bows before stepping onto the mat. In judo, this bow is called rei. It is a sign of respect toward the other player. The rulebook says when it happens, so it is the same in Paris, Tokyo or Chicago.
A referee stands between them. The referee says one Japanese word: hajime. It means begin. Before that word, the match has not started. After it, the rules are in force.
Later the referee will say sore made. It means that is all. The players bow again and leave the mat. A scoreboard shows who won and why. The judges and the rules decide, not the crowd.
None of this is left to chance. A written code says where the match happens, how it starts, how it ends and who decides. That code lets strangers from different countries meet on the same mat.
story.think: Why might players from different countries need the same written rules?

lessons.title: Every School Its Own Way
lessons.mainIdea: Before judo had a shared contest code, each jujutsu school had its own customs, so matches between schools had no common rules.
reading: In old Japan, each jujutsu ryu had its own customs. One school might allow things another school forbade. There was no single book that every school agreed to follow.

When students from two schools met, they had to agree on terms first. Sometimes they could not agree. Without shared rules, it was hard to say who had won fairly. It was also hard to keep people from getting hurt.
Kanō wanted judo contests to be fair and safer. The Kodokan wrote down rules for *contests*, or official matches. By about 1900, it had a written set of contest rules with a *referee* in charge.

words.d: an official match between two players, run by rules
the official who runs a match and makes sure the rules are followed

look.title: Two Schools Meet
look.text: Imagine two students from two different schools. The first school allows one thing. The second school forbids it. Nobody has written down which rule wins. A crowd waits to see who is the better student.
look.prompt: What problem do these two students have before they even start?

check.q: Why were matches between old jujutsu schools hard to judge?

check.why: Each ryu had its own customs, so there were no common rules to judge by.

check.q: About when did the Kodokan have written contest rules?
check.why: By about 1900, the Kodokan had written contest rules with a referee in charge.

lessons.title: Prizefights in England
lessons.mainIdea: In England in the 1700s and 1800s, boxers fought bare-handed for prize money under rules that changed over time.
reading: Far from Japan, England had its own fighting world. In the 1700s, boxers fought for money in *prizefights*. They fought with bare hands, so this is called *bare-knuckle* boxing. Many prizefights were against the law, but crowds still came.

In 1743, a London boxer named Jack Broughton wrote a short set of rules for his boxing hall. They are among the first written boxing rules. In 1838, a longer set called the London Prize Ring Rules came out.
Under these older rules, a round ended when a boxer went down. A fight could go on for many rounds and last for hours. Serious injuries were common. People began to ask for safer rules.

words.d: a boxing match fought for money
boxing with bare hands and no gloves
rules for bare-knuckle boxing first published in England in 1838

check.q: Who wrote a set of boxing rules in 1743?

check.q: Under the old prize ring rules, when did a round end?
check.why: Under the older rules, a round ended when a boxer went down.

lessons.title: A Page with Twelve Rules
lessons.mainIdea: The Queensberry Rules of 1867 were written by John Graham Chambers and named for the Marquess of Queensberry who backed them.
reading: In 1867, a new set of boxing rules was published in England. It had twelve short rules. A sportsman named John Graham Chambers wrote them. They carry the name of John Sholto Douglas, the ninth *Marquess* of Queensberry, who supported them.
So the rules are named for their backer, not their writer. That happens often in history. A famous name can help a new idea spread. People still call them the *Queensberry Rules*.
The rules asked boxers to wear *gloves* of good quality. They set the ring at 24 feet across. They called for a fair stand-up boxing match. These rules shaped modern boxing.

words.d: a title for a British noble; the Marquess of Queensberry lent his name to the 1867 rules
twelve boxing rules published in England in 1867 that called for gloves and timed rounds
padded coverings for the hands; the Queensberry Rules required them

look.title: From the Queensberry Rules
look.text: The match is to be a fair stand-up boxing match in a 24-foot ring, or as close to that size as possible. Rounds last three minutes, with one minute between rounds. Gloves must be fair-sized and of good quality.
look.cite: The Queensberry Rules, drawn up by John Graham Chambers, published in England, 1867
look.prompt: Name two things this rulebook sets that the old prize ring rules left open.

check.q: Who wrote the Queensberry Rules?
check.why: John Graham Chambers wrote them. The Marquess of Queensberry lent his name.

check.q: How many rules were in the 1867 Queensberry Rules?
check.why: The Queensberry Rules had twelve short rules.

check.q: How big a ring did the Queensberry Rules ask for?
check.why: The rules asked for a 24-foot ring.

lessons.title: Rounds and a Count
lessons.mainIdea: The Queensberry Rules set timed rounds, a rest between them and a ten-second count after a fall.
reading: The old prize ring had no clock for rounds. The Queensberry Rules changed that. Each *round* lasted three minutes. Then the boxers rested for one minute.
The rules also added a *count*. If a boxer went down, he had ten seconds to get up on his own. If he could not, the other boxer won. This gave every match a clear end.
A clock made boxing easier to judge. It also made matches shorter and more alike from place to place. Many other sports later used timed rounds or periods in the same way.

words.d: one timed part of a boxing match
the ten seconds a boxer who is down has to get up under the Queensberry Rules

look.title: The Clock in the Queensberry Rules
look.prompt: How many seconds is a round plus the rest after it?

check.q: How long was a round under the Queensberry Rules?
check.why: The rules set rounds of three minutes.

check.q: What was the count?
choices: ten seconds for a fallen boxer to get up
check.why: A boxer who went down had ten seconds to get up.

check.q: What did a clock change about boxing?
choices: It made matches shorter and easier to judge.
check.why: Timed rounds made matches shorter, more alike and easier to judge.

lessons.title: Gloves Win the Title
lessons.mainIdea: In 1892, the heavyweight title changed hands in a gloved fight, and amateur boxing grew under the new rules.
reading: For years, bare-knuckle and gloved boxing went on side by side. John L. Sullivan was the last bare-knuckle heavyweight champion. In 1892, in New Orleans, he lost the title to James J. Corbett. They fought with gloves under Queensberry rules.
Clubs for *amateurs* also grew. An amateur takes part for sport, not for money. In 1880, the Amateur Boxing Association was founded in England. It held yearly championships.
Boxing joined the Olympics in 1904 at St. Louis. Women waited much longer. Women's boxing first became an Olympic event in 2012 in London. That was 108 years after men's boxing began at the Games.

words.d: a person who takes part in a sport for its own sake, not for money
the class for the heaviest boxers

lessons.title: A Start and an End
lessons.mainIdea: Judo rules give every match a clear start and end, with a bow and set words from the referee.
reading: Judo contests follow a set order. Players bow at the edge of the mat and again facing each other. This bow is called *rei*. In judo schools, it is described as a sign of respect for the other player.
The referee starts the match with the word *hajime*, meaning begin. The word matte means wait, and it pauses the match. The words sore made mean that is all, and they end it.

These words are Japanese, and they stayed Japanese as judo spread. A referee in Brazil, France or the United States uses the same words. Shared words help players who speak different languages understand the match.

words.d: the bow in judo, described in judo schools as a sign of respect
the Japanese word a judo referee uses to begin a match; it means begin

look.title: Words from the Referee
look.text: Hajime means begin. Matte means wait. Sore made means that is all. A player from Brazil and a player from Korea hear these same three words in every judo contest, in every country.
look.prompt: Why might judo keep these words in Japanese everywhere instead of translating them?

check.q: What does hajime mean?
check.why: Hajime is the referee's word to begin the match.

check.q: What is rei?
check.why: Rei is the bow, described in judo schools as a sign of respect.

check.q: Why do judo referees everywhere use the same Japanese words?
choices: Because judo is only held in Japan.
Because shared words help players who speak different languages.
check.why: Using the same words in every country helps players from anywhere understand the match.

lessons.title: Matched by Weight
lessons.mainIdea: Weight classes group players of similar size, a rule that grew from four Olympic judo groups in 1964 to seven for men and seven for women.
reading: Early judo had no weight classes. Kanō taught that skill could beat size. Big and small players met in the same contests. The All-Japan Judo Championships, first held in 1930, still have no weight classes.

Many people thought size made contests unfair. At the 1964 Olympics, judo used three weight classes plus an open class. Over time, more classes were added. Today Olympic judo has seven *divisions* for men and seven for women.
Boxing and wrestling also use weight classes. The idea is the same in each sport. A *weigh-in* before the contest checks that each player is in the right group.

words.d: one group in a sport, such as a weight class
the check of each player's weight before a contest

look.title: Two Kinds of Contest

look.prompt: What does each kind of contest test? Which seems fairer to you, and why?

check.why: Olympic judo has seven weight divisions for men and seven for women.

check.q: What is a weigh-in?
choices: a check of a player's weight before a contest
check.why: A weigh-in checks that each player belongs in the right weight group.

check.q: What did Kanō teach about size?
choices: Size was the only thing that mattered.
check.why: Kanō taught that skill could beat size, so early judo had no weight classes.

lessons.title: One Blue, One White
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1990s, the world judo federation approved a blue jacket so judges and fans could tell the two players apart.
reading: For most of judo's history, both players wore white. A judo uniform is called a *judogi*. It has a heavy cotton jacket, pants and a belt. White judogi stayed the custom at the Kodokan.

When two players in white move fast, it can be hard to tell them apart. In the 1990s, the world judo federation approved a *blue judogi*. In top contests, one player now wears blue and one wears white.

Not everyone liked the change. Some in Japan wanted to keep white as a tradition. Supporters said blue helped judges, fans and television viewers. The debate shows that rules can carry feelings as well as facts.

words.d: the judo uniform: a heavy cotton jacket, pants and a belt
a blue judo uniform used in top contests so the two players look different

look.title: Watching on a Screen
look.text: You are watching a judo match on a small screen. Both players wear white. They move fast. Now imagine the same match with one player in blue. You can follow each player without guessing.
look.prompt: Who gains the most from the blue jacket: the players, the judges or the audience? Explain.

check.q: What is a judogi?
check.why: A judogi is the judo uniform: jacket, pants and belt.

check.q: Why was the blue judogi approved?
choices: to help people tell the two players apart
check.why: Blue and white jackets help judges, fans and viewers tell players apart.

check.q: Why did some people in Japan object to blue?
choices: They wanted to keep white as a tradition.
check.why: Some wanted to keep the white judogi as a tradition.

lessons.title: Bodies That Keep the Rules
lessons.mainIdea: International federations write and update the rules for their sports so contests match from country to country.
reading: A *federation* is a group of national bodies that agree to share one set of rules. The International Judo Federation, or IJF, was founded in 1951. It writes the rules for world judo contests. It held the first World Judo Championships in Tokyo in 1956.
Other arts have their own federations. The International Fencing Federation was founded in Paris in 1913. World Taekwondo was founded in 1973. Each one keeps a *rulebook* and updates it.
Federations also decide who may enter, how referees are trained and how records are kept. The Olympics works with these federations. Without one, a sport cannot easily join the Games.

words.d: a group of national bodies that agree to share one set of rules
a written set of rules that everyone in a sport agrees to follow

lessons.title: Judo After 1945
lessons.mainIdea: After World War II, martial arts were stopped in Japanese schools for several years, then judo returned as a sport.
reading: Japan lost World War II in 1945. The Allied forces, led by the United States, then *occupied* Japan until 1952. The occupation leaders worried that martial arts had been used to train young people for war.
For several years, martial arts training was stopped in Japanese schools. Judo leaders argued that judo was a sport and a form of education. Around 1950, judo came back into schools.
Judo's written rules helped make that case. A sport with a rulebook, a referee and weight rules looked like school sport, not war training. Within twenty years, Tokyo hosted Olympic judo.

words.d: when another country's forces take control of a place for a time
the world war from 1939 to 1945

look.title: Making the Case
look.text: Picture a judo teacher in about 1949. She shows an official a book of contest rules. It names a referee, a start word and an end word. It lists what is not allowed. She says: this is a sport for students.
look.prompt: How could a written rulebook help judo return to schools?

check.q: Until when did Allied forces occupy Japan after World War II?
check.why: The occupation of Japan lasted from 1945 to 1952.

check.q: About when did judo return to Japanese schools?
check.why: Around 1950, judo came back into Japanese schools.

check.q: How did a rulebook help judo after the war?
choices: It hid judo from the government.
It showed judo was a school sport, not war training.
check.why: Rules, a referee and set limits made judo look like school sport, not war training.

lessons.title: Judo Clubs in America
lessons.mainIdea: Japanese immigrants brought judo to the United States, and their clubs kept going even during the World War II camps.
reading: Judo reached the United States in the early 1900s. In 1904, a Kodokan teacher named Yamashita Yoshitsugu taught judo to President Theodore Roosevelt at the White House. Japanese immigrants also opened judo clubs in cities like Seattle, San Francisco and Los Angeles.

In 1942, President Franklin Roosevelt signed *Executive Order 9066*. It led the government to force about 120,000 Japanese Americans from the West Coast into camps. Most were American citizens. Judo clubs were started inside several camps, such as Manzanar in California.
After the war, judo grew across the country. Many judo clubs in America today trace their start to Japanese American teachers. In 1988, the United States government formally apologized for the camps.

words.d: the 1942 order that led to forcing Japanese Americans into camps
a person who moves to a new country to live

check.why: Executive Order 9066 led to about 120,000 Japanese Americans being forced into camps.

review.why: Each code gave matches set limits, a clear start and a clear end.
